title: Networking 06: Ch1 History, Summary and Wireshark

questions.q: In 1961, whose queueing-theory work showed that packet switching is effective?
questions.explain: 1961: Kleinrock's queueing theory showed packet switching is effective. Baran (1964) worked on packet switching for military networks.

questions.q: Baran's 1964 work applied packet switching to which kind of network?
questions.explain: 1964: Baran, packet switching in military nets. The Hawaii satellite network was ALOHAnet (1970).

questions.q: Which sequence is in correct chronological order?
choices: Baran's military packet switching -> Kleinrock's queueing theory -> first ARPAnet node operational -> ARPAnet conceived
ARPAnet conceived -> Kleinrock's queueing theory -> Baran's military packet switching -> first ARPAnet node operational
Kleinrock's queueing theory -> Baran's military packet switching -> ARPAnet conceived -> first ARPAnet node operational
Kleinrock's queueing theory -> ARPAnet conceived -> Baran's military packet switching -> first ARPAnet node operational
questions.explain: 1961 Kleinrock, 1964 Baran, 1967 ARPAnet conceived by the Advanced Research Projects Agency, 1969 first ARPAnet node operational.

questions.q: ARPAnet was conceived by the Advanced Research Projects Agency in 1967, and its first node became operational in 1969.
questions.explain: Both dates are correct: conceived 1967, first node operational 1969.

questions.q: What was the name of the first host-to-host protocol, introduced on ARPAnet in 1972? (acronym or full name)
questions.explain: NCP, the Network Control Protocol, was the first host-host protocol (1972). TCP/IP was not deployed until 1983.

questions.q: Which of these happened in 1972?
choices: NCP introduced as the first host-host protocol
questions.explain: 1972 brought the public ARPAnet demo, NCP, the first e-mail program, and a 15-node ARPAnet. TCP/IP was deployed in 1983, Ethernet came in 1976, and SMTP was defined in 1982.

questions.q: How many nodes did ARPAnet have in 1972?
questions.explain: ARPAnet had 15 nodes in 1972. By 1979 it had grown to 200.

questions.q: What did Cerf and Kahn contribute in 1974?
questions.explain: 1974: Cerf and Kahn designed an architecture for interconnecting networks. Their internetworking principles define today's Internet architecture.

questions.q: Which of these are Cerf and Kahn's internetworking principles?
choices: Minimalism, autonomy: no internal changes required to interconnect networks
Centralized control by a single authority
questions.explain: The four principles are minimalism/autonomy, a best-effort service model, stateless routing, and decentralized control. Guaranteed delivery and centralized control are the opposite of what they proposed.

questions.q: Under Cerf and Kahn's 'minimalism, autonomy' principle, what must an existing network do internally before it can be connected to the internetwork?
choices: Switch its internal routing to stateless routing
Nothing: no internal changes are required to interconnect networks
Adopt Ethernet as its link technology
Hand control to a central coordinating authority
questions.explain: Minimalism and autonomy mean each network keeps running as it is. No internal changes are needed to interconnect it.

questions.q: Under Cerf and Kahn's principles, routers keep per-connection state so they can guarantee that every packet is delivered.
questions.explain: Their principles call for stateless routing and a best-effort service model, so routers keep no per-connection state and delivery is not guaranteed.

questions.q: Where was Ethernet developed in 1976?
questions.explain: 1976: Ethernet at Xerox PARC.

questions.q: What was ALOHAnet (1970)?
choices: The first national academic network in the U.S.
A proprietary architecture from a computer vendor
questions.explain: ALOHAnet was a satellite network in Hawaii, built in 1970.

questions.q: Which of these were proprietary network architectures of the late 1970s?
questions.explain: DECnet, SNA and XNA were the proprietary architectures of the late 1970s. NSFnet, CSnet and BITnet were national networks of the 1980s.

questions.q: How many nodes did ARPAnet have in 1979?
questions.explain: ARPAnet grew from 15 nodes in 1972 to 200 nodes in 1979.

questions.q: In what year was TCP/IP deployed?
questions.explain: TCP/IP was deployed in 1983, the same year DNS was defined.

questions.q: What was DNS defined for in 1983?
questions.explain: 1983: DNS was defined to translate host names into IP addresses. FTP handles file transfer (1985) and SMTP handles e-mail (1982).

questions.q: Which e-mail protocol was defined in 1982? (acronym)
questions.explain: SMTP, the e-mail protocol, was defined in 1982.

questions.q: What was added to TCP in 1988?
questions.explain: 1988: TCP congestion control.

questions.q: Which of these was defined earliest?
questions.explain: SMTP came in 1982, DNS in 1983, FTP in 1985 and TCP congestion control in 1988.

questions.q: Which of these were new national networks of the 1980s?
questions.explain: The new national networks of the 1980s were CSnet, BITnet, NSFnet and Minitel. DECnet was a late-1970s proprietary architecture and ALOHAnet was a 1970 satellite network in Hawaii.

questions.q: By the end of the 1980s, roughly how many hosts were connected to the confederation of networks?
questions.explain: About 100,000 hosts by the end of the 1980s. 200 was ARPAnet's node count in 1979, about 50 million hosts was the late-1990s/2000s figure, and about 15 billion devices was the 2023 figure.

questions.q: Who created HTML and HTTP?
questions.explain: Berners-Lee created HTML and HTTP in the early 1990s. Bush (1945) and Nelson (1960s) developed the earlier idea of hypertext.

questions.q: The idea of hypertext was invented along with the Web in the early 1990s.
questions.explain: Hypertext came well before the Web: Bush in 1945 and Nelson in the 1960s. The Web built on that idea using HTML and HTTP.

questions.q: What did the NSF do in 1991?
choices: Lifted restrictions on commercial use of NSFnet
questions.explain: In 1991 the NSF lifted restrictions on commercial use of NSFnet, opening the way to commercialization. NSFnet itself was decommissioned in 1995.

questions.q: In what year was NSFnet decommissioned?
questions.explain: NSFnet was opened to commercial use in 1991 and decommissioned in 1995.

questions.q: Which Web browser appeared in 1994 and later led to Netscape?
questions.explain: 1994: Mosaic, which later became Netscape. The Web was commercialized in the late 1990s.

questions.q: Which of these describe the Internet in the late 1990s to 2000s?
choices: New killer apps such as instant messaging and P2P file sharing
Network security moves to the forefront
An estimated 50 million hosts and 100 million+ users
More mobile than fixed devices on the Internet
questions.explain: The first four describe the late 1990s and 2000s. Mobile devices outnumbered fixed ones in 2017, and SDN arrived in 2008. Both belong to the 2005-present era.

questions.q: ARPAnet was decommissioned in the early 1990s.
questions.explain: ARPAnet was decommissioned in the early 1990s, as commercial use of the Internet began.

questions.q: In what year did software-defined networking (SDN) appear?
questions.explain: SDN appeared in 2008.

questions.q: Why do service providers such as Google, Facebook and Microsoft build their own networks?
choices: To replace DNS with a proprietary naming system
To bypass the commercial Internet and connect 'close' to end users, giving near-instantaneous access to search, social media and video
Because the commercial Internet does not support TCP/IP
To avoid having to use broadband home access
questions.explain: These providers bypass the commercial Internet so they can connect close to end users and give them near-instant access to their content.

questions.q: By 2017, more mobile devices than fixed devices were connected to the Internet.
questions.explain: With the rise of smartphones, mobile devices outnumbered fixed devices on the Internet by 2017.

questions.q: Approximately how many devices were attached to the Internet in 2023, in billions?
questions.explain: About 15 billion devices were attached to the Internet in 2023.

questions.q: What does it mean for an enterprise to run its services 'in the cloud'?
choices: It runs them on infrastructure from providers such as Amazon Web Services or Microsoft Azure instead of only on its own machines
It serves them only over satellite links
It runs them on a private, proprietary network architecture such as SNA
It runs them on peer-to-peer file-sharing networks
questions.explain: Since 2005, enterprises have increasingly run their services in the cloud, on providers such as Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure.

questions.q: Which developments belong to the 2005-present era?
choices: Aggressive deployment of broadband home access (10-100's of Mbps)
Increasingly widespread high-speed wireless access: 4G/5G and WiFi
NSF lifting restrictions on commercial use of NSFnet
questions.explain: Broadband, 4G/5G and WiFi, and smartphones belong to the 2005-present era of scale, SDN, mobility and cloud. TCP/IP was deployed in 1983, and the NSFnet change came in 1991.

questions.q: Which two layers of the ISO/OSI reference model are not in the Internet protocol stack?
questions.explain: OSI has seven layers. The Internet stack has five and does not include the presentation and session layers.

questions.q: Which OSI layer lets applications interpret the meaning of data, for example through encryption, compression and machine-specific conventions?
questions.explain: The presentation layer lets applications interpret the meaning of data, including encryption, compression and machine-specific conventions.

questions.q: Which OSI layer provides synchronization, checkpointing and recovery of data exchange?
questions.explain: The session layer provides synchronization, checkpointing and recovery of data exchange.

questions.q: An Internet application that needs data compression can hand that job to the Internet protocol stack's presentation layer.
questions.explain: The Internet stack has no presentation layer. Presentation and session services, if needed, must be implemented in the application itself.

questions.q: Which list gives the seven OSI layers from top to bottom?
choices: application, session, presentation, transport, network, link, physical
application, presentation, session, network, transport, link, physical
application, presentation, session, transport, network, link, physical
presentation, application, session, transport, link, network, physical
questions.explain: Top to bottom: application, presentation, session, transport, network, link, physical.

questions.q: In the OSI model, which layer sits directly between the presentation layer and the transport layer?
questions.explain: The order is presentation, then session, then transport.

questions.q: How many layers does the ISO/OSI reference model have?
questions.explain: Seven: the five Internet-stack layers plus presentation and session.

questions.q: What is the transport-layer unit (transport header Ht plus message M) called?
questions.explain: Application: message (M). Transport: segment (Ht+M). Network: datagram (Hn+Ht+M). Link: frame (Hl+Hn+Ht+M).

questions.q: What is the network-layer unit, made of the network header Hn plus a transport segment, called?
questions.explain: The network layer adds Hn to the segment, which produces a datagram.

questions.q: Which shows the contents of a link-layer frame, from the front of the frame to the back?
questions.explain: Each lower layer puts its header in front of what it receives from above, so the link header Hl is outermost: Hl Hn Ht M.

questions.q: As data moves down the stack at the source, each layer adds its own header to the unit it receives from the layer above.
questions.explain: That is encapsulation. M becomes a segment (+Ht), then a datagram (+Hn), then a frame (+Hl), and the frame is sent over the physical layer.

questions.q: At the destination, the network layer receives a datagram (Hn Ht M) from the link layer. What does it pass up to the transport layer?
questions.explain: At the destination each layer removes its own header. The network layer strips Hn and passes the segment (Ht M) up to transport.

questions.q: At the source, the application passes message M to the transport layer. What does the transport layer pass down to the network layer?
questions.explain: The transport layer adds its header Ht to M, making a segment (Ht M), and passes it down to the network layer.

questions.q: What does Wireshark's packet capture (pcap) component receive from the host's protocol stack?
choices: Only the application-layer messages of the web browser
A copy of every Ethernet frame sent or received
Only IP datagrams addressed to the host
Only the TCP segments that arrive with errors
questions.explain: pcap taps the link (Ethernet) layer and gets a copy of every Ethernet frame the host sends or receives.

questions.q: Which two components make up Wireshark?
questions.explain: Wireshark has two parts. Packet capture (pcap) collects copies of frames, and the packet analyzer works on what pcap captured.

questions.q: Wireshark takes frames out of the protocol stack, so applications such as a web browser do not receive the traffic while it is being captured.
questions.explain: pcap receives a copy of each frame. The original frames still pass through the stack as usual, so the browser or e-mail client keeps working.

questions.q: At which layer of the host's protocol stack does Wireshark's packet capture get its copies?
questions.explain: pcap copies the Ethernet frames at the link layer. Because a frame contains everything above it, the analyzer can see every layer's headers.

questions.q: Wireshark captures an Ethernet frame that carries part of a web page request. Given how encapsulation works, what does that captured frame contain?
choices: The IP and TCP headers, but not the HTTP message
The Ethernet header, IP header, TCP header and the HTTP message data
questions.explain: A frame is Hl Hn Ht M. A captured Ethernet frame therefore holds the link (Ethernet), network (IP) and transport (TCP) headers plus the application message, which is why a single capture shows every layer.

questions.q: In the Wireshark diagram, where does each Wireshark component sit relative to the application/OS boundary?
choices: Both components run inside the web browser
Packet capture sits at the OS level next to the protocol stack, and the packet analyzer runs as an application above it
The packet analyzer is inside the OS, and packet capture runs on the router
Both components run on the router, not the host
questions.explain: pcap sits below the application/OS line, beside the stack, where it can copy frames. The packet analyzer is an application above it that receives pcap's output. Both run on the host itself.
